William Pitt the Younger. Britain's youngest Prime Minister at twenty-four, dominating Parliament through the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars.

Pitt became Prime Minister at age twenty-four and served for nearly nineteen years total, second only to Walpole in longevity. His tenure from 1783 to 1801 and again from 1804 to 1806 made him the architect of Britain's fiscal system and the principal strategist against Napoleon.

He reformed the tax system, introducing the income tax temporarily during the Napoleonic Wars to finance military campaigns against France. This innovation in taxation would become a permanent feature of the British state. Pitt advocated for parliamentary reform and Catholic emancipation, though he could not achieve either during his lifetime. Both causes were championed by successors who built on the foundations he laid.

Pitt orchestrated the Third Coalition against Napoleon in 1805 and subsidized allied powers, spending vast sums to contain French expansion. The burden of financing this vast war effort took a toll on his health. His phrase upon hearing of Napoleon's victory at Austerlitz captured the strategic despair of the moment. He reportedly said, roll up the map of Europe, for it will not be needed for ten years.

Pitt died in office in 1806, worn down by the strain of wartime leadership. He was just forty-six years old, exhausted by the weight of steering Britain through its greatest existential challenge.
